entry: Property of sets in mathematics that measures their size, roughly the number of objects they contain, which may be infinite. Two [[Set (mathematics)|sets]] have the same cardinality if their objects can be paired one-to-one, with none left unpaired. For finite sets, cardinality equals the usual count of elements. Infinite sets are measured by the [[Aleph number|Aleph numbers]], which extend the process of counting. The [[Natural number|natural numbers]] have cardinality ℵ₀, and a set is countably infinite if it can be paired one-to-one with them. The [[Real number|real numbers]] are uncountable, a result proved by diagonal arguments, which show that there are different sizes of infinity. [[Georg Cantor|Cantor]] introduced cardinality formally to mathematics in the late 19th century. Whether the reals have cardinality ℵ₁ is the continuum hypothesis, which is neither provable nor disprovable in standard set theories such as [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]].

Branch of [[Medicine|medicine]] concerned with disorders of the [[Heart|heart]] and the cardiovascular system. A sub-specialty of internal medicine, it covers the diagnosis and treatment of congenital heart defects, [[Coronary artery disease|coronary artery disease]], [[Heart failure]], valvular heart disease and electrophysiology. Physicians in the field are called cardiologists. Surgery such as coronary artery bypass grafting and valve replacement belongs to cardiothoracic surgery, although cardiologists increasingly perform less invasive procedures, including cardiac catheterization and pacemaker implantation. In the United States, training consists of a three-year residency in internal medicine followed by a three-year fellowship in cardiology. [[Cardiovascular disease]] is the leading cause of death worldwide, responsible for an estimated 19.2 million deaths in 2023, about 32% of all global deaths. Willem Einthoven invented the electrocardiograph in 1901.

Goods transported by land, water or air, while freight refers to their conveyance. In economics, freight is goods carried at a freight rate for commercial gain. Reusable multimodal containers are also called cargo, as are the goods stored in them. Bulk cargo, such as salt, [[Oil|oil]], grain and [[Gypsum|gypsum]], is carried unpackaged, while break-bulk or general cargo is handled in individual pieces. Since the 1960s, the volume of break-bulk cargo has declined enormously worldwide in favor of containers. Aircraft were first used to carry mail as cargo in 1911, and large planes such as the [[Boeing 747]] carry standardized unit load devices. Trains move large numbers of containers from [[Port|ports]].

[[Merchant ship]] designed to carry goods, commodities and materials across seas and oceans. Cargo ships carry most of the world's freight by volume, ranging from small coastal vessels to ocean-going carriers. Container ships carry all their load in standardized intermodal containers and now carry most seagoing non-bulk cargo. Bulk carriers transport unpackaged commodities, while [[Tanker (ship)|tankers]] carry liquids and gases in bulk. Feeder vessels, with an average capacity of 300 to 1,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU), collect containers from different ports and transport them to central terminals for larger liners. Modern cargo ships are built of welded steel and fitted with cranes or gantries, whereas older ones were made of wood. Larger cargo ships are generally operated by shipping lines.

Sea of the North [[Atlantic Ocean|Atlantic Ocean]] in the tropics of the Western Hemisphere. It is bounded by the [[Greater Antilles]] to the north, the [[Lesser Antilles]] to the east, [[South America]] to the south and [[Central America]] and the Yucatán Peninsula to the west. The sea covers about 2,754,000 sq km (1,063,000 sq mi), and its deepest point, the Cayman Trough, lies 7,686 m (25,217 ft) below sea level. The sea contains the world's second-largest barrier reef, which runs 1,000 km (620 mi) along the coasts of Mexico, Belize, Guatemala and Honduras. The name derives from the Caribs, one of the region's dominant native peoples at the time of European contact. After [[Christopher Columbus]] landed in the [[The Bahamas|Bahamas]] in 1492, Spain colonized the area first, followed by England, the Dutch Republic, France and Denmark, and the sea became a busy route for trade and piracy. As of 2015, the area had 22 island territories and bordered 12 continental countries.

Large, complex [[Nebula|nebula]] in the constellation Carina, also known as NGC 3372. It lies in the Carina–Sagittarius Arm of the Milky Way, about 8,500 light-years (2,600 pc) from [[Earth]]. It contains the Carina OB1 association and several open clusters with numerous [[Star|O-type stars]] and [[Wolf–Rayet star|Wolf–Rayet stars]]. Although about four times as large as the [[Orion Nebula]] and brighter, it is less well known because of its southern location. Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille discovered it in 1752 from the [[Cape of Good Hope]]. Its central star, Eta Carinae, is a hypergiant with an estimated mass of 100 to 150 times that of the Sun, and the Homunculus Nebula around it is believed to have been ejected in an outburst in 1841. The [[James Webb Space Telescope|James Webb Space Telescope]] included the nebula among five cosmic objects in its first science images.

German engine designer and automotive engineer. His Benz Patent-Motorwagen of 1885 is considered the first practical modern [[Car|automobile]] and the first car put into series production. Benz received a [[Patent|patent]] for the motorcar in 1886, the year he first publicly drove it. His company, Benz & Cie., based in Mannheim, was the world's first automobile plant. In 1926 it merged with Daimler Motoren Gesellschaft to form Daimler-Benz, which produces the [[Mercedes-Benz]] brand. Benz is widely regarded as the father of the automobile industry. He studied mechanical engineering at the Karlsruhe polytechnical school.

Finnish military commander and statesman. Baron Mannerheim led the White forces in the [[Finland|Finnish]] Civil War of 1918 and served as regent of Finland from December 1918 to July 1919. He became commander-in-chief of the Finnish Defence Forces when the Soviet Union invaded in November 1939, starting the [[Winter War]]. He then led the Continuation War of 1941–1944, an invasion of the [[Soviet Union]] alongside [[Nazi Germany]]. In 1944 Parliament unanimously appointed him president, and he oversaw peace negotiations with the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom. He became Finland's only field marshal in 1933. Mannerheim is often called the father of modern Finland, and he spent his last years in a Swiss sanatorium, where he wrote his memoirs.

German mathematician. He made fundamental contributions to elliptic functions, dynamics, [[Differential equation|differential equations]], [[Determinant|determinants]] and [[Number theory|number theory]]. He earned a [[Doctor of Philosophy|doctorate]] in 1825 and became a tenured professor of mathematics at the University of Königsberg in 1829, holding the chair until 1842. After a breakdown from overwork in 1843, he lived in [[Berlin]] as a royal pensioner. His royal grant was cut off after the Revolution of 1848 but was restored through the intervention of [[Alexander von Humboldt]]. He died of a [[Smallpox|smallpox]] infection, and the crater Jacobi on the Moon is named after him.

Swiss psychiatrist, psychotherapist and founder of [[Analytical psychology|analytical psychology]]. He worked as a research scientist at the Burghölzli psychiatric hospital in [[Zurich|Zurich]] under Eugen Bleuler. Initially a close colleague of [[Sigmund Freud]], who arranged his appointment as president of the International Psychoanalytical Association, Jung parted from Freud over theoretical differences and developed analytical psychology as a separate system. Central to it is individuation, the lifelong process of differentiating the self from its conscious and unconscious elements. He created concepts including archetypes, the collective unconscious, synchronicity, the psychological complex, and [[Extraversion and introversion|extraversion and introversion]]. His 1926 treatment of the American businessman Rowland Hazard played a role in the chain of events leading to the founding of Alcoholics Anonymous. Many of his works were not published until after his death.

American former track and field athlete. A dominant sprinter and [[Long jump|long jumper]], Lewis won nine Olympic gold medals, one Olympic silver medal and 10 World Championships medals, including eight gold. He is one of two athletes to win gold in the same individual athletics event at four [[Olympic Games]], along with discus thrower Al Oerter. He topped world rankings in the 100 m, 200 m and long jump events from 1981 to the early 1990s, and his 65 consecutive long jump victories over ten years is among the sport's longest undefeated streaks. He was named World Athlete of the Century by the International Association of Athletics Federations. After retiring he became an actor, and in 2011 he sought a New Jersey Senate seat but was removed from the ballot over residency. He is head track and field coach at the University of Houston.

Swedish biologist and physician. He formalized [[Binomial nomenclature|binomial nomenclature]], the modern system of naming organisms, and is known as the father of modern [[Taxonomy|taxonomy]]. Born in Råshult in Småland, he studied at Uppsala University and began giving lectures in botany there in 1730. He published the first edition of *Systema Naturae* in the [[Netherlands]] during a stay abroad from 1735 to 1738. Afterward he became professor of medicine and botany at Uppsala and made several journeys through Sweden to find and classify plants and animals. He was ennobled in 1761 as Carl von Linné. Linnaeus is also considered one of the founders of modern [[Ecology|ecology]], and he placed humans within the order [[Primate|Primates]], alongside apes and monkeys.

American comedian, actor, writer and director whose career spanned seven decades. He contributed sketch material to *Your Show of Shows* and *Caesar's Hour* and, with [[Mel Brooks]], created the *2000 Year Old Man* comedy routines. He created and produced *The Dick Van Dyke Show* (1961–1966). As a director he made comedies including *Oh, God!* (1977), and he directed several films starring [[Steve Martin]]. He won 11 Primetime Emmy Awards.

American psychologist and one of the founders of [[Humanistic psychology|humanistic psychology]]. He is known for person-centered [[Psychotherapy|psychotherapy]], an approach applied to counseling, education, organizations and group settings. Rogers is considered one of the founding figures of psychotherapy research. He received the American Psychological Association's Award for Distinguished Scientific Contributions in 1956 and its Award for Distinguished Professional Contributions to Psychology in 1972. He was one of several psychologists who worked on Project MK-Ultra, which developed techniques of psychological torture. One study ranked him the sixth most eminent psychologist of the 20th century.

American astronomer, planetary scientist and science communicator. He was David Duncan Professor of Astronomy and Space Sciences at [[Cornell University|Cornell University]], where he directed the Laboratory for Planetary Studies. He played an active role in [[NASA|NASA]]'s Mariner, Viking and Voyager programs and was a founding member and first president of the Planetary Society. He co-wrote and narrated the 1980 television series *Cosmos: A Personal Voyage*, which won two Emmy Awards and a Peabody Award. His book *The Dragons of Eden* won the Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction. He published more than 600 scientific papers and articles, and in *The Demon-Haunted World* he promoted skepticism and [[Critical thinking|critical thinking]]. He played a major role in developing the Voyager Golden Record, a message carried aboard the Voyager spacecraft.

Danish film director and screenwriter. Widely considered one of the greatest filmmakers, Dreyer was noted for emotional austerity, slow and stately pacing, and themes of social intolerance and the power of evil. His silent film *The Passion of Joan of Arc* (1928), noted for its [[Cinematography|cinematography]] and use of close-ups, was voted the ninth-best film by critics in a 2012 *Sight & Sound* poll. Other notable films include *Michael* (1924), *Vampyr* (1932), *Day of Wrath* (1943), *Ordet* (1955) and *Gertrud* (1964).

Prussian army officer and military theorist. His unfinished treatise *On War* (*Vom Kriege*), published posthumously in 1832–34, is a seminal work on [[Military strategy|military strategy]]. He stressed the psychological and political aspects of war and the "fog of war", the incomplete and often erroneous information under which commanders must decide quickly. He argued that war could not be reduced to mapwork and geometry. His best-known aphorism holds that "war is the continuation of policy with other means." He fought in the [[Napoleonic Wars]] and later directed the Prussian War College.

Italian football manager and former midfielder. As a manager he has won the [[UEFA Champions League|UEFA Champions League]] five times, a record, and he is the only manager to have won league titles in Italy, England, France, Germany and Spain. His clubs include [[AC Milan]], Chelsea, Paris Saint-Germain, Real Madrid and Bayern Munich. He was appointed head coach of the Brazil national team in 2025.

Mexican business magnate, investor and philanthropist. From 2010 to 2013, [[Forbes|Forbes]] ranked him the richest person in the world. His fortune derives mainly from telecommunications, including América Móvil, which operates throughout [[Latin America|Latin America]], and Telmex, the Mexican telephone company he acquired after its privatization. Telmex maintained a virtual [[Monopoly|monopoly]] for many years after his acquisition. Through his conglomerate, Grupo Carso, he holds interests in construction, manufacturing, retail, real estate, mining, mass media and financial services. He accounts for 40 percent of the listings on the Mexican Stock Exchange.

American singer-songwriter and author. Her hits include "You're So Vain", which topped the Billboard Hot 100, and "Nobody Does It Better", the theme for the [[James Bond|James Bond]] film *The Spy Who Loved Me*. Her song "Let the River Run", from *Working Girl*, won an Academy Award, a Golden Globe and a [[Grammy Awards|Grammy]]. She was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2022.

*Opéra comique* in four acts by Georges Bizet, with a libretto by Henri Meilhac and Ludovic Halévy adapted from Prosper Mérimée's novella. Set in southern Spain, it tells how the soldier Don José, seduced by the fiery Carmen, deserts his duties and, after she turns to the bullfighter Escamillo, kills her in a jealous rage. Its premiere at the Opéra-Comique in Paris on 3 March 1875 shocked audiences with its lawlessness and an onstage murder, and most reviews were critical. The opera gained its reputation through productions outside France and was not revived in Paris until 1883. The "Habanera", "Seguidilla" and "Toreador Song" are among the best-known operatic arias. Critics regard it as a bridge between the opéra comique tradition and the [[Realism (arts)|realism]] of late 19th-century Italian opera.

Classical music system of South India, one of the two main subgenres of [[Indian classical music|Indian classical music]], alongside Hindustani music. It is associated mainly with Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Telangana, and most of its compositions are in Telugu and Sanskrit. Its foundations, śruti (pitch), svara (note), rāga (melodic mode) and tala (rhythmic cycle), are shared with Hindustani music. Carnatic music emphasizes vocal music and improvisation, and is usually performed by a vocalist accompanied by a violin, a mridangam and a tambura drone. Its core repertoire is the kriti, a form developed between the 14th and 20th centuries. The Trinity of Carnatic music, including [[Tyagaraja|Tyagaraja]], [[Muthuswami Dikshitar|Muthuswami Dikshitar]] and Syama Sastri, are among its most important composers. The greatest concentration of musicians is in [[Chennai|Chennai]].

Reddish-brown [[Chalcedony|chalcedony]] used as a semiprecious stone. Its color comes from iron oxide impurities and ranges from pale orange to almost black. It is closely related to sard, which is generally harder and darker, and the two names are often used interchangeably. Carnelian has been worked since the [[Bronze Age|Bronze Age]], and in [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]] it was carved into amulets and seals. It has been found in Brazil, India, Indonesia, Iran and Germany.

Festive season at the close of the Christian pre-Lenten period, known as Shrovetide in some areas. It consists of Shrove Sunday, Shrove Monday and Shrove Tuesday, which is called [[Mardi Gras|Mardi Gras]] in some places. Carnival features public parades, street parties and entertainments, with elaborate costumes and [[Mask|masks]] that let people set aside everyday roles. Participants indulge in food and drink, such as pancakes and doughnuts, before the Lenten fast. The term is used mainly in areas with a large Catholic presence and in [[Greece|Greece]], while Protestant areas use Shrovetide and Slavic Orthodox nations celebrate Maslenitsa. The name is traced to the Latin *carnem levare*, "to remove meat." Notable modern carnivals include the [[Samba|samba]] parades of [[Rio de Janeiro|Rio de Janeiro]] and the masked balls of [[Venice|Venice]].

Order of placental mammals specialized primarily for eating flesh. Its members, called carnivorans, number at least 293 species, making it the sixth-largest order of mammals. Carnivorans are found on every major landmass and in habitats ranging from polar regions to the Sahara Desert and the open seas. The order has two suborders: Feliformia, containing the true [[Felidae|felids]] and several cat-like animals, which are mostly confined to the Old World; and Caniformia, containing the true [[Canidae|canids]] and many dog-like animals, including bears, mustelids and pinnipeds. Carnivora originated in the late Paleocene, about 60 million years ago.
